<reason>A set the decision rule early (three conjunctive pillars, one falls and the motion fails) and then attacked with concrete, plausible, closed-book-appropriate grounding: Spain's default predating its rate surge by a decade, Wales as PRO's own "soft" blueprint underdelivering, Brazil's repeal as evidence that presumption can damage trust where trust is thinnest. B answered the Spain point cleverly ("the network made the default usable") and landed a genuinely good turn — opt-in already converts the unregistered's silence into a veto, so the equity objection cuts both ways. But B never supplied a case where the presumption plausibly did independent work, and then conceded under A's Q1 that the isolating experiment "almost never exists," which A converted into a burden failure on the "measurably increase" pillar. A's vise — the softer the system, the less it moves; the harder it moves, the more it costs ethically — was never dissolved; B's reply that "soft does not mean powerless" was assertion rather than demonstration. A's strongest original move was that the gain and the wrong are the same set of cases: any extra organ must come from a family that would otherwise have declined. B's closing tried to sever those cases (ignorance-driven declines, not known objections), which was the right target, but A's closing pre-empted and reframed it vividly: same daughter, same ignorance, opposite outcome — the blank registry is evidence of nothing, so the surplus lives entirely inside ambiguity. A's execution cost is real: rebuttal 1 was clipped for exceeding the cap, and the "most patients" scope point was slightly pedantic against B's reasonable reframe toward listed patients. Both sides answered pressure with proper A1:/A2: labels and stayed disciplined about sourcing. A simply made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's answer to its own Q2 and the closing follow-through: PRO needs the default powerful enough to move rates yet gentle enough to move no one who meant no, so every extra yes comes from exactly the hesitant, uninformed family whose consent is ethically weakest. B's attempted severance in closing — the extra organ comes from ignorance, not from a known objector — was the right rejoinder, but A's "same daughter, same ignorance, opposite outcome" recast it as uncertainty merely being scored in favour of retrieval, leaving the ethics pillar contested at best.</best_rebuttal>
